mission_2.prediction: I chose A* and DFS. I predict A* will finish sooner on the constrained map. In Mission 1, A* found the shortest route of 24.5 m, while DFS found a much longer route of 104 m, about 4.2 times optimal, because it follows one branch deep into the maze before reaching the goal. The robot moves at the same speed limit with the same controller on both routes, so a longer route with more turns should take more time to drive. DFS should also have to slow down for more turns, since the controller slows for sharp corners.
mission_2.performance: On the constrained map, A* succeeded with an elapsed time of 89.5 s and a distance of 23.9 m. DFS ended in a timeout at 179.9 s after travelling only 44.4 m of its 104 m planned route. This supports my prediction that A* would finish sooner. The clearest evidence is DFS’s mean tracking error of 7.14 m, compared with 0.27 m for A*. The robot was far from its planned line for most of the run, and its executed path stops partway through the maze instead of reaching the goal. At 0.30 m/s the 104 m route needs about 347 s, which is longer than the 180 s limit, so DFS could not finish.
mission_2.choice: I would choose Nav2 Smac 2D. It succeeded on both maps, finishing the open map in 35.2 s and the constrained map in 73.8 s, the fastest of all seven methods on both. Compared with my A*, which took 46.3 s on the open map and 89.5 s on the constrained map, Nav2 drove a shorter route on the constrained map, 20.6 m against 23.9 m. Its tracking error was slightly higher, 0.283 m against 0.272 m, so it did not follow its path better. It did keep more distance from the walls, with a minimum static clearance of 0.26 m against 0.11 m for A*. The advantage that matters most for a delivery robot is that combination of speed and extra clearance, because a robot that stays further from walls and obstacles is safer around people. PRM was a close alternative, at 75.0 s on the constrained map and with the lowest tracking error, 0.253 m. Each cell was a single trial, so none of this is a proven success rate.
